stages.title: Atoms and matter
stages.hook: Take a sand castle. Break it into smaller and smaller bits. What do you think the tiniest bit is?
explain: Everything around you is made of matter. Water, air, wood and your own body are all matter.
Matter is made of tiny pieces called atoms. Atoms are far too small to see, even with a school magnifying glass.
Atoms stick together in groups. A group of atoms is called a molecule. Water is made of molecules, and each one has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

example.q: A water molecule has 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. How many atoms is that in one molecule?

analogies.home: A wall is made of many bricks. Matter is made of many atoms.
analogies.nature: A beach is made of grains of sand. A drop of water is made of molecules.
analogies.farm: A field of wheat is many small plants. A bag of flour is many tiny pieces.
analogies.music: A song is made of notes. Matter is made of atoms.

stages.mnemonic: Atoms are the tiny bricks that build everything.
terms: Anything that takes up space and has mass.
A tiny building block of matter.
A group of atoms joined together.

misc.wrong: Atoms are big enough to see.
misc.right: Atoms are far too tiny to see. We learn about them using special machines and clever ideas.

stages.limits: This is a simple picture. Real atoms are not like tiny hard balls, but the picture helps us start.

stages.title: Atomic nuclei
stages.hook: Imagine a pea in the middle of a huge football stadium. What if the pea is the heart of an atom?
explain: Every atom has a tiny centre called the nucleus. It is like the heart of the atom.
The nucleus is made of even smaller bits. Some are called protons and some are called neutrons.
Around the nucleus, even tinier bits called electrons zoom about. Nearly all of the atom's weight is in the nucleus.
The nucleus is very, very small compared with the whole atom. Most of an atom is empty space.

example.q: An atom has 1 nucleus. The nucleus has 2 protons and 2 neutrons. How many bits are in the nucleus?

analogies.sport: The nucleus is like the pea in the middle of a stadium. The stadium is the whole atom.
analogies.nature: A peach has a hard stone in the middle. An atom has a nucleus in the middle.
analogies.city: A city has a small busy centre. The atom has a small, heavy nucleus.
analogies.home: A cherry has one small stone inside. An atom has one small nucleus inside.

stages.mnemonic: Nucleus: the Neat little centre, heavy as a stone in a cherry.
terms: The tiny centre of an atom.
A tiny bit that zooms around the nucleus.

misc.wrong: The nucleus is most of the atom's size.
misc.right: The nucleus is tiny. It holds nearly all the weight, but takes up very little of the space.

stages.title: Energy in nature
stages.hook: What makes the wind blow, the plants grow and the rivers flow? Is there one thing behind them all?
explain: Energy is what makes things happen. It lets things move, grow and get warm.
The Sun gives us light and heat. Plants use sunlight to grow. Animals eat plants and get energy from food.
Moving water and wind carry energy too. People use these to make electricity.
Energy is never made from nothing. It changes from one kind to another.

example.q: Sunlight helps a plant grow. A goat eats the plant and runs. Where did the goat's running energy first come from?
steps: So the energy first came from the Sun.

analogies.farm: Sun, then grass, then cow, then milk. The energy passes along.
analogies.sea: Wind pushes a sail boat. The wind's energy moves the boat.
analogies.home: A battery gives energy to a toy so it can move.
analogies.nature: A river flows down a hill. The moving water has energy.

stages.title: Different types of energy
stages.hook: A torch glows, a fan spins and a heater warms. Is it the same energy in all three?
explain: Energy comes in different kinds. Light energy helps us see. Heat energy keeps us warm. Movement energy is in anything that moves.
Sound is energy too. So is electricity, which runs through wires to light our homes.
Some energy is stored. A stretched rubber band, a battery and food all store energy for later.
Energy can change from one kind to another. A bulb changes electricity into light and a little heat.

example.q: A toaster gets hot when it is on. What kind of energy changes into heat?
steps: A toaster is plugged into a wall.
The toaster changes electricity into heat.

stages.title: Radiation in everyday life
stages.hook: Sunlight, radio and the warmth of a fire all travel through space. Are they all kinds of radiation?
explain: Radiation is energy that travels out from something. Light from the Sun is a kind of radiation. So is the warmth you feel from a fire.
Radio waves, the ones in your phone, are radiation too. Most everyday radiation is harmless in small amounts.
Some radiation comes from tiny atoms. This is called ionising radiation. It is also found naturally in rocks, soil and space.
The amount we meet each day is very small. Too much of any radiation can be harmful, so we take care.

example.q: A person sits near a warm fire. What kind of radiation do they feel?
steps: The fire warms the person without touching.
The energy travels through the air.

stages.title: Radiation safety awareness
stages.hook: You are sitting by a very hot fire. How can you keep yourself comfortable?
explain: To stay safe from strong radiation, remember three ideas: time, distance and shielding.
Time: spend less time near it. Distance: stay far away. Shielding: put something solid between you and it.
At a fire, you move back and you put up a screen. Strong radiation works in a similar way.
People who work with strong radiation are trained. They use special signs and tools. If you see a warning sign, stay away and tell a grown-up.

example.q: A fire is too hot on your face. Name one way to feel less heat.
steps: Heat is strongest close to the fire.

analogies.sea: At the beach we wear a hat and sit under an umbrella.

stages.title: Nuclear energy applications
stages.hook: Nuclear energy can light cities, but can it do other jobs too? What might they be?
explain: Nuclear energy comes from the nucleus of an atom. A lot of energy is stored there.
The most well-known use is making electricity in power stations. Some ships and submarines are also powered by nuclear energy.
Other uses help people every day. Doctors use it to see inside the body. Farmers use it to study crops. Factories use it to check welds in pipes.
Every use has benefits and some risks, so people use strict safety rules.

example.q: A power station and a hospital both use nuclear science. Name one job in each place.
steps: A hospital helps doctors see inside the body.
Both use ideas from the nucleus.
example.a: Electricity at the power station; body pictures at the hospital

stages.limits: People disagree about how much nuclear power we should use. We look at benefits and risks.

teach.topic: What nuclear energy is used for
teach.model: Nuclear energy comes from the nucleus of atoms. It makes electricity in power stations. It also helps in hospitals, farms and factories. Every use has benefits and some risks, so safety rules matter.

stages.title: Nuclear medicine introduction
stages.hook: How can a doctor see inside your body without cutting you open?
explain: Doctors can see inside the body using special pictures. Some of these use a very small, safe amount of radiation.
In nuclear medicine, a patient may get a tiny amount of a special substance that gives off radiation. A camera then sees where it goes.
This can show how organs like the heart or bones are working. A different kind of treatment can also use radiation to help treat some illnesses, under the care of a doctor.
The amounts are chosen with great care, and the benefit to the patient should be bigger than the risk.

example.q: A doctor uses a special camera to see how a heart works. Is it cutting the patient open?
steps: The camera sits outside the body.
It picks up signals from a tiny amount of tracer.

analogies.nature: A firefly lights up so you can follow it in the dark. A tracer is a little like that for a camera.
analogies.city: A traffic camera shows where cars go. A tracer shows where a substance goes.
analogies.home: A torch lets you see in a dark room.
analogies.tech: A phone camera sees light. A special camera sees radiation from a tracer.

stages.mnemonic: Tiny tracer, special camera, clear picture.
terms: Medicine that uses small amounts of radiation to find or treat illness.
A tiny amount of a substance that can be followed by a camera.
A picture of the inside of the body.

misc.wrong: Any radiation in a hospital is dangerous.
misc.right: Doctors choose tiny, careful amounts. The benefit is bigger than the small risk.

stages.limits: This is a story, not advice for any person. A real doctor decides what is best for a real patient.

stages.title: Nuclear power stations
stages.hook: A kettle boils water and makes steam. What if a power station did the same thing, only much bigger?
explain: A nuclear power station makes heat from atoms. The heat boils water into steam.
The steam pushes a wheel with blades called a turbine. The turbine turns a generator, and the generator makes electricity.
Then the steam is cooled back into water and used again.
Power stations have thick walls and many safety layers. They are watched by trained people all day and night.

example.q: Put the steps in order: steam turns turbine, heat is made, generator makes electricity, water boils.

analogies.home: Steam from a kettle can make a lid rattle. In a station, steam spins a wheel.
analogies.nature: A river turns a water wheel. Steam turns a turbine.
analogies.city: Wires from the station carry electricity to homes.
analogies.farm: A windmill pumps water. A turbine makes electricity.

terms: A wheel with blades that spins.
Water that has boiled into gas.
Several protections, so one failure is not enough to cause harm.

misc.right: They do not burn anything. The heat comes from changes in atoms.

stages.limits: Stations are complex. This is a simple picture of how they work.

teach.model: Atoms give heat. The heat boils water into steam. The steam spins a turbine, and the turbine turns a generator. The generator makes electricity. Many safety layers protect people.
